summary: Lists requirements for gathering and transferring location information securely while protecting the privacy of the people involved. It focuses on authorization, security and privacy needs, in particular for the Geopriv Location Object and the protocols that use it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Apps that know where you are can be handy but also creepy. This says what rules are needed so location data is only shared with people you approve.

questions: what is the geopriv location object
what is a geopriv location object
what is a privacy rule in geopriv
subtitle: What a secure, privacy-respecting way to share a person's location must provide.

tldr.problem: Location-based services need to gather and pass on where someone is, but doing so can expose that person's privacy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for a Geopriv Location Object and the protocols that carry it: user-controlled Privacy Rules, support for unlinked pseudonyms, and authentication, integrity, confidentiality and replay protection.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol, and it has been updated by RFC 6280 and RFC 7459.

today: RFC 3693 is an Informational requirements document and has been updated by RFC 6280 and RFC 7459. It was not obsoleted according to the metadata.

sections.title: Overview and Principles
sections.content:
Location-based services, such as navigation, emergency services and equipment tracking, need the location of a Target. Collecting and passing that information has privacy implications. The goal is to protect privacy according to Privacy Rules set by the Rule Maker, usually the user.

Six principles guide the requirements: the Location Object must be securely transmitted; user-controlled Privacy Rules decide who gets location and for what use; rules can filter by reducing precision or resolution (for example, coworkers learn only the city); the Location Object should carry a limited core set of rules; location should not be tied to a real identity where appropriate; and users may hide identities even from other protocol participants.
sections.eli5: You should decide who knows where you are, and how exactly. A friend might only learn your city, not your street.

sections.title: The Four Geopriv Entities
sections.content:
The basic architecture has four entities. The Location Generator (LG) determines the Target's location and creates Location Objects. The Location Server (LS) receives them, applies the rules and notifies recipients. The Location Recipient (LR) receives notifications. The Rule Holder (RH) houses the Privacy Rules, which are populated by the Rule Maker, and the LS can pull them or the RH can push them.

These need not be separate machines: the interfaces could be internal to one device, and in some designs the LG, RH and LS are the same device. The RFC states that rules MUST be authenticated and protected.
sections.eli5: One person finds you, a gatekeeper decides what to tell, someone asks, and a rulebook says what is allowed. All can be the same helper wearing four hats.

sections.title: Key Terms: Objects, Rules and Pseudonyms
sections.content:
A Sighting is the first determination of location from non-public information. The Location Object (LO) conveys location information, an identity or pseudonym, time, core Privacy Rules and authenticators; most fields are optional. A using protocol is one that reads or modifies the LO, as opposed to one that merely transports it.

A Privacy Rule regulates collection, use, disclosure and retention of location, and the RFC says rules must be obeyed, not treated as advisory. An unlinked pseudonym is an identifier whose link to its holder is initially unknown to anyone but the holder or a trusted server. Flows are trusted if a prior contract covers location privacy, and non-trusted otherwise.

The RFC lists four situations that might override a Rule Maker: emergency services, legal interception, an employer or location owner, and a government in non-emergency cases. The working group had to facilitate only the emergency case.
sections.eli5: The location note is an envelope with your stand-in nickname on it, not your real name, and a rulebook that must be followed.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The Location Object requirements: Geopriv MUST define one LO that every entity supports, it MUST be extensible, usable in protocols such as HTTP and SIP, and usable securely on constrained devices. It MUST have fields for the Target identifier, recipient identity, credential and proof of possession, location, location data type, timing and rules, plus security headers and a version number. At least one location data type must be supported by all receivers, and the RFC says there SHOULD be two: coordinates and civil locations.

For rules, a Location Server's decision to provide location MUST be based on the Rule Maker's rules. A Location Generator MUST follow the Rule Maker's instructions even without the full rules, for example by sending only to a URI the Rule Maker designates. Geopriv MUST specify a limited rule language.

For security, the LO MUST support unlinked pseudonyms and fields for mutual end-point authentication, data integrity, confidentiality and replay protection. Geopriv MUST specify minimum mandatory-to-implement crypto, and the protocol SHOULD allow a bypass if authentication fails in an emergency call. A non-requirement: bridging to non-IP networks such as the PSTN.
sections.eli5: The rule list says the location note must be extensible, lockable, sealed so nobody can alter or replay it, and able to hide your real name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only information inside the Location Object is protected by the Rule Maker's rules; other headers and objects generally are not, so Geopriv may not defend the Target against general traffic analysis. Rules are authenticated according to where they live: non-public Rule Holders typically use a MAC or signature, public ones are typically digitally signed, and rule fields in an LO are secured with the LO.

For emergency calls where authentication fails, the Rule Maker could write a rule to send the location anyway or to let the call fail, and a default of sending only to an emergency center is reasonable. Unlinked pseudonyms are needed for anonymity, and hiding the recipient from the Location Server prevents inferring habits from who asks. The RFC also notes unintended targets, such as the driver of a tracked rental car, whose privacy is affected.
sections.eli5: The seal only covers the location note itself. Someone watching who sends mail to whom could still learn things, so there are extra tricks like nicknames.

sections.title: Open Issues for Later
sections.content:
The RFC lists issues left for later. A Location Object may hold multiple location fields or multiple representations of the same position. Fields could show that one location is a translation of another. The format of timing information is out of scope.

The LO MUST NOT have a truth flag, since Geopriv must be silent on whether the location is true. Who defines identifiers is also open: letting the using protocol define the name space eases embedded authentication, while letting the rules choose gives the user control of anonymity. Pseudonyms should be changed regularly, since identifying the user behind one can be very simple.
sections.eli5: Some questions were put in a to-do pile, like how to write down the time, and whether to let the note say it is telling the truth. The answer to the last one is no.
